newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW-Telegroup aims to make inroads in France.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Telegroup aims to make inroads in France.

text.p: Telegroup Inc aims to make big inroads in the French telecommunications market from next year, becoming a niche player in international communications and largely dropping its current activity as a call-back service.
"We realised that call-back services are largely death," said Georges Apple, European Director, Business Development, in an interview.
From January 1, 1998, Telegroup will have a French operating licence to use leased lines which will allow it to buy telecom capacity at wholesale rates and sell at, higher retail prices.
It has been competing with France Telecom since 1993 with so-called call-back services, undercutting France Telecom by some 50 percent in price.

"Basically what we did was exporting the U.S. dial tone," Apple said. A customer would call the number of a computer in New York, hang-up and wait for the computer to call back within seven to 12 seconds.

The company currently has 40,000 subscribers in France which make 2.5 million minutes of calls per month. This makes Telegroup currently the second-biggest international operator in France, Apple said, albeit very far behind France Telecom.
Telegroup recently changed its call-back technology, letting customers call a number in Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris instead of New York, but Apple said the margins for call-back were eroding.

"In the last few months there have been a number of developments that went against us. France Telecom dropped its international rates, parliament passed a bill on value added tax on call back and the dollar lost some 10 to 12 percent against the franc," Apple said.

"Because we had no intention of dropping from the marketplace we slashed our rates as well, and our margins. Even today we can still offer savings of between 15 and 40 percent depending on the destination," he added.
Call-back will remain in place for mobile communications because there is still a big price difference there but the future for Telegroup in France lies in leased-lines.
As a so-called L34 operator it can offer telecom services without owning a network of its own.

It will have to negotiate with network owners, either France Telecom, Cegetel or Bouygues, to get access to the so-called "local loop" where the subscribers are to carry the calls from the home or office to the leased line.
In principle, Telegroup would have to be treated as equal in France to other new entrants such as Cegetel or Bouygues but Apple said he feared this would not be the case.

"From 1998, if you want to call somebody in France using France Telecom you dial a 10-digit number starting with a zero, if you want to use Cegetel you would use a 10-digit number starting with, say, a one. But for Telegroup you will have to use a long number before the number of your correspondent," Apple said.
He quoted France Telecom as saying it was not technically feasible at the moment to allocate more first numbers for phone numbers.

"They recently changed the French systems to 10-digits and the entire switch-over operation lasted some 90 seconds. If they can achieve a technological feat like that, I can't see why they cannot treat us equal with a short number," Apple said.
"They do not want to treat us as equal," he added, declining to indicate whether he would seek arbitration by the French telecoms regulator ART.

Apple was also reluctant to give sales, profit or market share goals, saying the group wanted to be "the best" in its niche. "It's quiet respectable to be a niche player. The market is set to grow rapidly due to the competition and lower prices. If the market were to grow to $100 billion than even if we had only a few percent of that we would be doing fine," Apple said.
